example.english: The clown is very funny.
example.fact: 丑 also names the second of the twelve Chinese zodiac branches, associated with the Ox.

components.note: 少 (few, little) — suggests something lacking or insufficient, the root idea behind 'inferior.'
力 (lì) gives a sound that's a close but not exact match for liè — they share the initial and a similar rhyme.

example.english: The weather outside is very bad.
example.fact: 劣 rarely stands alone in modern Mandarin — it usually appears in words like 恶劣 (èliè, 'terrible') or 优劣 (yōuliè, 'pros and cons').

components.note: 木 (wood) — axe handles, stalks, and boughs are all made of or belong to wood.
可 (kě) gives the sound — a close match for kē, differing only in tone.

example.english: Ke is a surname.
example.fact: Today 柯 is mostly seen as a surname; its older meaning 'axe handle' is rarely used in modern speech.

etymologyHint: A hand with a dot indicating where the pulse can be felt, about an inch up the wrist

components.note: 寸 pictures a hand with a small mark near the wrist, showing the point about an inch up where a pulse can be felt — the image behind its meaning 'inch, small.'

example.pinyin: Yí cùn dàyuē shì sān límǐ.
example.english: One cun is about three centimeters.
example.fact: 寸 is a traditional Chinese unit of length, about one-tenth of a 尺 (chi) — roughly 3.3 centimeters.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — throwing is an action done with the hand.
乃 (nǎi) gives a sound distantly related to rēng, having drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Tā rēng le yí gè qiú.
example.english: She threw a ball.
example.fact: 扔 is a common everyday verb for throwing or tossing something away.

components.note: 目 (eye) — staring is something done with the eyes.
丁 (dīng) gives the sound — an exact match for 盯.

example.english: He keeps staring at his phone.
example.fact: 盯 describes a fixed, unblinking gaze — a stronger, more focused word than the general verb 看 ('to look').

example.english: Others shouldn't insult you.
example.fact: 辱 rarely appears alone in modern speech; it most often combines with 侮 to form 侮辱 (wǔrù), 'to insult.'

meanings: (bound form) alone; single; one of a pair

components.note: 匹 pictures a roll of cloth folded over itself — the image behind its meaning 'bolt of cloth,' later extended to a classifier for horses.

example.english: I saw a horse.
example.fact: 匹 is the special measure word used for horses — one of many classifiers in Mandarin tied to specific kinds of nouns.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 俱 describes people being 'all together.'
具 (jù) gives the sound — an exact match for 俱.

example.english: Their club is very famous.
example.fact: 俱 rarely stands alone today — it's most familiar inside 俱乐部 (jùlèbù), the transliteration of English 'club.'

etymologyHint: To separate 刂 two alternatives 辛

components.note: 辛 appears on both sides of the character, representing the two things being told apart.
刂 (knife) sits between them, picturing the act of cutting things apart — giving 辨 its meaning 'to distinguish.'

example.english: We need to learn to tell true from false.
example.fact: 辨 usually pairs with 别 to form 辨别 (biànbié), 'to distinguish' — and it's easy to confuse with the similar-looking 辩 (biàn, 'to debate').

etymologyHint: To want 我 food 饣; 我 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 饣 (food) — 饿 relates to a need for food.
我 (I, self) suggests personal want or need — paired with food, giving 饿 its meaning 'hungry.'

example.english: I'm very hungry, I want to eat.
example.fact: 饿 is one of the first adjectives beginners learn to describe how they feel before a meal.

components.note: 虫 (insect) — a bee is a kind of insect.
夆 (féng in related characters) gives a sound close to fēng, sharing the same rhyme.

example.english: Bees make honey.
example.fact: 蜂 alone is a bound form meaning 'bee, wasp'; the everyday standalone word for a bee is 蜜蜂 (mìfēng).

components.note: 口 (mouth) — an interjection like 'oh' is spoken aloud.
我 (wǒ) gives a sound distantly related to ó, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: Oh, I understand now.
example.fact: 哦 is a mouth-radical interjection whose meaning comes almost entirely from tone and context, not from its written parts.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh) — 腔 names a hollow space inside the body.
空 (kōng) gives a sound distantly related to qiāng, having drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Yīshēng jiǎnchá le wǒ de kǒuqiāng.
example.english: The doctor examined my oral cavity.
example.fact: 腔 names a hollow space in the body — 口腔 (kǒuqiāng, 'oral cavity') is the term you'll hear at the dentist.

components.note: 阝 (from 邑, city) — an old tie to a place name, per its 'city' etymology.
有 (yǒu) gives a sound close in initial to yù, though the rhyme has drifted over time.

example.english: He's feeling gloomy today.
example.fact: 郁 shows up most often today in 郁闷 (yùmèn), a common colloquial word for feeling gloomy or stifled.

meanings: used in 潰膿|溃脓[hui4 nong2]

components.note: 氵 (water) — 溃 originally described a river bursting its banks.
贵 (guì) gives the sound — a close match for kuì, sharing the same rhyme.

example.pinyin: Tā yālì tài dà, kuài bēngkuì le.
example.english: He has too much pressure, he's about to break down.
example.fact: 溃 appears in the common word 崩溃 (bēngkuì), 'to collapse' or 'to break down,' whether structurally or emotionally.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — caution here is expressed carefully in what one says.
堇 (jǐn) gives the sound — an exact match for 谨.

example.english: You must be careful when driving.
example.fact: 谨 usually appears with 慎 in 谨慎 (jǐnshèn), 'careful, prudent' — a word often used for safety advice.

components.note: 米 (grain, rice) — 糟 originally named the dregs left over from making rice wine.
曹 (cáo) gives a sound close to zāo, sharing the same rhyme and tone.

example.pinyin: Zāogāo, wǒ wàng le dài yàoshi!
example.english: Oh no, I forgot to bring my keys!
example.fact: 糟 is best known through 糟糕 (zāogāo), a common exclamation meaning 'oh no!' or 'terrible!'

components.note: 艹 (grass, plant) — kudzu is a climbing plant.
曷 (hé) gives a sound close to gé, sharing the same rhyme and tone.

example.english: His surname is Ge.
example.fact: Today 葛 is mainly encountered as a surname; its original meaning refers to kudzu, a climbing plant.

etymologyHint: Grass 艹 growing in a field 田

components.note: 艹 (grass) — the young green shoots of a growing plant.
田 (field) — together with the grass above, the picture of a seedling growing in a field, giving 苗 its meaning 'sprout.'

example.english: The little sprout is growing quickly.
example.fact: 苗 pictures grass 艹 growing up out of a field 田 — and the same character also names the Miao ethnic group.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh) — intestines are a body organ.
昜 (yáng in related characters) gives a sound distantly related to cháng, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: I like eating sausage.
example.fact: 肠 literally means 'intestines,' but its most common everyday use is inside 香肠 (xiāngcháng), 'sausage.'

components.note: 心 (heart) — jealousy and dread are both feelings of the heart.
己 (jǐ) gives the sound — a close match for jì, sharing the initial and rhyme.

example.hanzi: 中国人吃饭时有一些忌讳。
example.pinyin: Zhōngguó rén chīfàn shí yǒu yìxiē jìhuì.
example.english: Chinese people have some taboos around eating.
example.fact: 忌 often appears in 忌讳 (jìhuì), 'taboo,' and 禁忌 (jìnjì), describing things to avoid out of caution or custom.

components.note: 氵 (water) — sliding and slipping evoke the smoothness of water.
留 (liú) gives the sound — a close match for liū, differing only in tone.

example.english: He slipped away quietly.
example.fact: 溜 describes a smooth, slippery motion — used both for literally sliding (溜冰, 'to skate') and for slipping away unnoticed.

components.note: 鸟 (bird) — 鸿 names a kind of large wild bird.
江 (jiāng) gives a sound distantly related to hóng, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: Wild geese can fly long distances.
example.fact: 鸿 names a large wild swan or goose in classical Chinese, and today lives on mostly in literary words like 鸿雁 (hóngyàn) and in given names.

etymologyHint: A hand 寸 holding a goblet 良 of wine 罒

components.note: 寸 here depicts a hand.
良 pictures a goblet — together, a hand holding a ceremonial wine goblet, the image behind 爵's original meaning 'noble rank.'

example.english: He likes listening to jazz music.
example.fact: 爵 originally named a feudal noble rank; today it's most often seen in 爵士乐 (juéshìyuè), the Chinese term for 'jazz' — a phonetic borrowing of the English word.

components.note: 鸟 (bird) — 鹏 names a giant mythical bird.
朋 (péng) gives the sound — an exact match for 鹏.

example.pinyin: Péng shì chuánshuō zhōng de dà niǎo.
example.english: Peng is a giant bird from legend.
example.fact: 鹏 comes from Chinese mythology, describing an enormous bird able to fly vast distances — it also appears often in people's given names.

components.note: 鸟 (bird) — 鹰 names a bird of prey, the falcon or eagle.

example.english: The eagle is flying in the sky.
example.fact: 鹰, like eagles and hawks generally, is known for remarkably sharp eyesight.

meanings: (used in 籠子|笼子[long3 zi5]) large box

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — cages and steaming baskets were traditionally woven from bamboo.
龙 (lóng) gives the sound — an exact match for 笼.

example.pinyin: Bāozi shì yòng lóngzi zhēng de.
example.english: Baozi are steamed using a bamboo steamer.
example.fact: 笼 names both an animal cage and the bamboo steamer basket (蒸笼) used to cook dumplings and buns.

components.note: 丘 pictures two small hills side by side, giving its meaning 'hill, mound.'

example.pinyin: Yuǎnchù yǒu yí zuò xiǎo qiū.
example.english: There's a small hill in the distance.
example.fact: 丘 names a small hill or mound — smaller than a mountain (山) but rising above flat ground.

components.note: 木 (wood, tree) — cassia and osmanthus are both trees.
圭 (guī) gives the sound — a close match for guì, differing only in tone.

example.english: Osmanthus flowers are very fragrant.
example.fact: 桂 names the osmanthus tree (桂花), prized for its fragrant autumn blossoms, and is also the short name for Guangxi province.

components.note: 氵 (water) — growth and nourishment are tied to water.
兹 (zī) gives the sound — an exact match for 滋.

example.english: Drinking soup can nourish the body.
example.fact: 滋 often pairs with 养 to form 滋养 (zīyǎng), 'to nourish' — a nod to the water radical's link to growth.

components.note: 耳 (ear) — chatting involves listening as well as speaking.
卯 (mǎo) gives a sound distantly related to liáo, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: We are chatting.
example.fact: 聊 is best known through 聊天 (liáotiān), literally 'chatting with the sky' — one of the most common everyday verbs for chatting.

etymologyHint: A hand 扌 raised at the right time 当; 当 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 扌 (hand) — blocking something is done with the hand.
当 here contributes to the character's form, describing being raised up at the right moment.

example.english: He blocked the sunlight with his hand.
example.fact: 挡 describes physically blocking something, as in 挡住 (dǎngzhù), 'to block.'

meanings: head rope of a fishing net

components.note: 纟 (thread) — 纲 originally named the thick rope threading a fishing net together.
冈 (gāng) gives the sound — an exact match for 纲.

example.hanzi: 老师给我们一份课程大纲。
example.pinyin: Lǎoshī gěi wǒmen yí fèn kèchéng dàgāng.
example.english: The teacher gave us a course outline.
example.fact: 纲 originally meant the main rope of a fishing net; today it commonly means an 'outline' or 'guiding principle,' as in 大纲 (dàgāng).

components.note: ⺼ (flesh) — muscle is a kind of body tissue.
几 (jǐ) gives the sound — a close match for jī, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 运动可以让肌肉更强壮。
example.pinyin: Yùndòng kěyǐ ràng jīròu gèng qiángzhuàng.
example.english: Exercise can make muscles stronger.
example.fact: 肌 is the formal word for 'muscle,' almost always seen paired as 肌肉 (jīròu).

components.note: 艹 (grass, plant) — thatching and the caltrop plant are both plant-based.
次 (cì) gives the sound — a close match for cí, differing only in tone.

example.english: The character 'ci' is rarely used nowadays.
example.fact: 茨 historically referred to thatching material or the caltrop plant; today you'll mostly encounter it in old texts or place names.

meanings: (coll.) shell (of an egg, nut, crab etc)
case; casing; housing (of a machine or device)
etymologyHint: A shell discarded 冗 by a soldier 士

components.note: 士 here depicts a person, per the old story of a soldier discarding something.
冗 pictures something being tossed aside — together, a discarded shell, giving 壳 its meaning 'casing, shell.'

example.english: An egg's shell is very thin.
example.fact: 壳 names a hard outer casing, as in 蛋壳 (dànké, 'eggshell') or 外壳 (wàiké, the outer casing of a device).

components.note: 疒 (sickness) — a scar is a mark left by an injury or illness.
艮 (gèn) gives a sound close in rhyme to hén, though the initial consonant has drifted.

example.pinyin: Qiáng shàng liúxià le yí dào hénjì.
example.english: A mark was left on the wall.
example.fact: 痕 commonly appears in 痕迹 (hénjì), meaning 'trace' or 'mark' left behind by something.

components.note: 石 (stone) — early bowls were carved from stone or made of pottery.
宛 (wǎn) gives the sound — an exact match for 碗.

example.pinyin: Qǐng gěi wǒ yí gè wǎn.
example.english: Please give me a bowl.
example.fact: 碗 is the standard word — and measure word — for a bowl of rice, soup, or noodles.

components.note: 穴 pictures the mouth of a cave, with a peaked roof and an opening below — the image behind its meaning 'cave, den.'

example.english: The snake lives in a cave.
example.fact: 穴 alone means 'cave' or 'den' (as in 洞穴); the same character also names the acupuncture points used in traditional Chinese medicine.

meanings: used in 吊膀子[diao4 bang4 zi5]
etymologyHint: Flesh ⺼ beside 旁 the body; 旁 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: ⺼ (flesh) — 膀 names a part of the body.
旁 (beside) contributes to the character's form, describing something at the body's side, like the upper arm or a wing.

example.pinyin: Xiǎo niǎo de chìbǎng shòushāng le.
example.english: The little bird's wing is injured.
example.fact: 膀 appears in 翅膀 (chìbǎng), 'wing,' and also in 膀胱 (pángguāng), 'bladder' — note the different reading in that second word.

etymologyHint: To foresee ⺊ the dawn 早 coming; 早 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: ⺊ here suggests foreseeing or divining something ahead.
早 (early, dawn) contributes to the character's form — together, the image of foreseeing the dawn before it comes, giving 卓 its meaning 'outstanding, lofty.'

example.english: His achievements are outstanding.
example.fact: 卓 is most familiar today in 卓越 (zhuōyuè), 'outstanding, excellent.'

components.note: 贝 (shell, an ancient form of money) — 贤 ties moral worth to the idea of something valuable.

example.pinyin: Gǔdài yǒu hěn duō xiánnéng de rén.
example.english: In ancient times there were many virtuous and capable people.
example.fact: 贤 describes both moral virtue and ability — 贤能 (xiánnéng) praises someone who is both virtuous and capable.

etymologyHint: A person 卜 (altered form of 人) laying in bed 臣

components.note: 臣 here pictures a large, downcast eye, an old image tied to lying down or resting.
卜 (an altered form of 人, 'person') completes the picture of someone lying in bed, giving 卧 its meaning 'to lie down.'

example.english: My bedroom is very small.
example.fact: 卧 is most familiar today inside 卧室 (wòshì), 'bedroom' — literally the 'room for lying down.'

components.note: ⺼ (flesh) — a membrane is a kind of body tissue.
莫 (mò) gives the sound — a close match for mó, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 妈妈用保鲜膜包好食物。
example.pinyin: Māma yòng bǎoxiānmó bāo hǎo shíwù.
example.english: Mom wrapped the food with plastic wrap.
example.fact: 膜 names a thin membrane or film — 保鲜膜 (bǎoxiānmó) is the everyday word for plastic food wrap.

components.note: 殳 (tool, weapon) — resolve here is linked to the force of wielding a tool.
豙 (yì) gives the sound — an exact match for 毅.

example.english: Success requires perseverance.
example.fact: 毅 is almost always seen in 毅力 (yìlì), 'willpower, perseverance.'

etymologyHint: Silk 帛 inlaid with gold 钅; 钅 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 钅 (metal, gold) — 锦 describes cloth inlaid with gold thread.
帛 (silk) contributes to the character's form, naming the fine fabric being decorated.

example.pinyin: Zhè kuài bù shì jǐnduàn zuò de.
example.english: This fabric is made of brocade.
example.fact: 锦 names a fine silk brocade, and appears in the idiom 锦上添花 (jǐn shàng tiān huā), literally 'adding flowers to brocade' — meaning to make something already good even better.

components.note: ⺈ here pictures an open, exhaling mouth.
人 (person) completes the picture of someone yawning, an old image now used abstractly for 'lacking, owing.'

example.pinyin: Wǒ qiàn tā shí kuài qián.
example.english: I owe him ten yuan.
example.fact: 欠 means both 'to owe' money and 'to lack' something — the same character covers both senses.

meanings: (modal final particle similar to 呢[ne5] or 啦[la5])

components.note: 口 (mouth) — a spoken particle is voiced through the mouth.
里 (lǐ) gives the sound — a close match for lī, differing only in tone.

example.english: He still hasn't come yet.
example.fact: 哩 here functions as a colloquial sentence-final particle, similar to 呢 or 啦, adding a casual tone.

etymologyHint: Letters placed in a container 凵

components.note: 凵 pictures an open container — 函 shows letters or documents placed inside a case for safekeeping.

example.pinyin: Gōngsī fā lái le yì fēng gōnghán.
example.english: The company sent an official letter.
example.fact: 函 is a formal word for 'letter' or 'case' — used today in words like 函数 (hánshù, 'function' in math) and 公函 (gōnghán, 'official letter').

components.note: 艹 (grass) — 茫 originally described endless, boundless grassland.
汒 (a rare character) gives the sound — an exact match for 茫.

example.pinyin: Tā duì wèilái gǎndào hěn mímáng.
example.english: He feels lost about the future.
example.fact: 茫 is most familiar in 迷茫 (mímáng), 'confused, lost' — describing not knowing which way to turn.

components.note: 日 (sun) — 昂 originally described something rising, like the sun.
卬 (áng) gives the sound — an exact match for 昂.

example.english: This piece of clothing is very expensive.
example.fact: 昂 today is most familiar in 昂贵 (ángguì), 'expensive' — from its original sense of something held 'high.'

meanings: vassal state during the Zhou Dynasty (1046–256 BC)
etymologyHint: A kind of bitter 辛 grass 艹

components.note: 艹 (grass) — 薛 originally named a kind of bitter marsh grass.
辛 (bitter, harsh) contributes to the character's form, describing the plant's bitter taste.

example.english: Her surname is Xue.
example.fact: 薛 is used almost exclusively today as a surname; its older meaning refers to a kind of marsh grass.

components.note: 皮 (skin) — wrinkles form on the skin.
刍 (chú) gives a sound distantly related to zhòu, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: He frowned angrily.
example.fact: 皱 is most familiar in 皱纹 (zhòuwén), 'wrinkles,' and 皱眉 (zhòu méi), 'to frown.'

components.note: 大 (great, big) — boasting or praising both involve making something out to be great.
亏 (kuī) gives a sound close to kuā, sharing the initial consonant.

example.pinyin: Lǎoshī kuājiǎng le wǒ de zuòwén.
example.english: The teacher praised my essay.
example.fact: 夸 covers both 'to praise' (夸奖, kuājiǎng) and 'to boast, exaggerate' (夸张, kuāzhāng) — context tells the two apart.

meanings: short name for Henan 河南[He2 nan2]

components.note: 象 (elephant) — elephants once roamed the region now called Henan, tying the character to comfort and abundance.
予 (yǔ) gives the sound — a close match for yù, differing only in tone.

example.english: Henan province's short name is 'Yu.'
example.fact: 豫 is the official one-character abbreviation for Henan province, still used today on its car license plates.

etymologyHint: The stomach ⺼ behind the abdominal muscles 田

components.note: 田 here pictures the stomach itself, reused from its usual meaning 'field.'
⺼ (flesh) sits below, marking 胃 as a body part.

example.pinyin: Tā de wèi bú tài hǎo.
example.english: His stomach isn't very good.
example.fact: 胃 is the standard word for the stomach as a body organ.

etymologyHint: A tongue 千 sticking out of a mouth 口

components.note: 千 here pictures a tongue sticking upward.
口 (mouth) sits below it — together, a tongue sticking out of a mouth, giving 舌 its meaning.

example.english: A cow's tongue is very long.
example.fact: 舌 pictures a tongue sticking out of a mouth — cows are in fact known for having unusually long tongues.

components.note: 刂 (knife) — peeling is done with a blade or the fingers acting like one.
录 (lù) gives a sound distantly related to bō, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: I'm peeling an orange.
example.fact: 剥 is the standard verb for peeling or shelling something, from fruit to nuts.

components.note: 亻 (person) — pride and arrogance are human traits.
敖 (áo) gives the sound — a close match for ào, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他为自己的成绩感到骄傲。
example.pinyin: Tā wèi zìjǐ de chéngjì gǎndào jiāo'ào.
example.english: He feels proud of his achievements.
example.fact: 傲 almost always appears with 骄 in 骄傲 (jiāo'ào), 'proud' — which can mean either healthy pride or arrogance depending on context.

meanings: accounting form of the numeral ten
etymologyHint: To gather 合 things in one's hands 扌

components.note: 扌 (hand) — picking something up is done with the hand.
合 (to gather, combine) contributes to the character's form, describing the action of gathering things up.

example.hanzi: 他从地上拾起一枚硬币。
example.pinyin: Tā cóng dìshang shíqǐ yì méi yìngbì.
example.english: He picked up a coin from the ground.
example.fact: 拾 also serves as the formal, harder-to-forge way to write the number ten (十) on checks and receipts.

meanings: pit or hollow on the human body

components.note: 穴 (cave, hole) — a nest or den is a hollow, cave-like space.
呙 gives a sound close to wō, as it does in the related character 涡 (wō).

example.hanzi: 小鸟在树上做了一个窝。
example.pinyin: Xiǎo niǎo zài shùshàng zuò le yí gè wō.
example.english: The little bird made a nest in the tree.
example.fact: 窝 names a nest or den — and colloquially, staying home all day is jokingly called 'wō zài jiā lǐ.'

components.note: 目 (eye) — 睁 describes an action of the eyes.
争 (zhēng) gives the sound — an exact match for 睁.

example.hanzi: 早上他睁开眼睛，看到了阳光。
example.pinyin: Zǎoshang tā zhēngkāi yǎnjing, kàndào le yángguāng.
example.english: In the morning he opened his eyes and saw sunlight.
example.fact: 睁 is almost always used in 睁开 (zhēngkāi), 'to open (one's eyes).'

components.note: 扌 (hand) — carrying something along is done by hand.
隽 (juàn in related readings) gives a sound distantly related to xié, having drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Qǐng xiédài hǎo nǐ de hùzhào.
example.english: Please bring your passport with you.
example.fact: 携 often appears on travel signs in 携带 (xiédài), 'to carry along' — as in reminders to bring your ID or luggage.

etymologyHint: A hill 阝 where people are laid to rest 夌; 夌 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 阝 (hill) — a mausoleum was traditionally built into a hillside.
夌 (to ascend, climb) contributes to the character's form, describing the raised mound of the tomb.

example.pinyin: Běijīng yǒu zhùmíng de Shísān Líng.
example.english: Beijing has the famous Ming Tombs.
example.fact: 陵 specifically names a royal or notable person's tomb, as in 十三陵 (Shísān Líng), the Ming Tombs near Beijing.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — humming and groaning are vocal actions.
亨 (hēng) gives the sound — an exact match for 哼.

example.pinyin: Tā yìbiān zǒu yìbiān hēngzhe gē.
example.english: She hummed a song while walking.
example.fact: 哼 describes humming a tune or letting out a low groan of disapproval — the meaning depends on context.

meanings: generic term for cotton or kapok
etymologyHint: Silk 帛 picked off a tree 木

components.note: 木 (tree, plant) — cotton is a plant fiber.
帛 (silk, fine cloth) contributes to the character's form, tying the plant fiber to the idea of soft fabric.

example.english: In winter you need to cover yourself with a cotton quilt.
example.fact: 棉 is most familiar in 棉花 (miánhua), 'cotton,' and 棉被 (miánbèi), 'cotton quilt.'

components.note: 日 (sun) — clear weather means the sun is visible.
青 (qīng) gives the sound — a close match for qíng, differing only in tone.

example.english: The weather is very clear today.
example.fact: 晴 describes clear, sunny weather, as opposed to 阴 (yīn), 'overcast.'

components.note: 钅 (metal) — bells are made of metal.
令 (lìng) gives the sound — a close match for líng, differing only in tone.

example.english: The doorbell rang.
example.fact: 铃 names a small bell, as in 门铃 (ménlíng, 'doorbell') and 铃声 (língshēng, 'ringtone').

meanings: (of a form etc) to fill in

components.note: 土 (earth) — 填 originally meant to fill a space with earth or soil.
真 (zhēn) gives a sound distantly related to tián, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: Please fill out this form.
example.fact: 填 is most familiar in 填写 (tiánxiě), 'to fill out (a form),' and 填空 (tiánkòng), 'to fill in the blank.'

components.note: 饣 (food) — feeding animals means providing them food.
司 (sī) gives the sound — a close match for sì, differing only in tone.

example.pinyin: Nóngmín sìyǎng le hěn duō jī.
example.english: The farmer raises a lot of chickens.
example.fact: 饲 is almost always seen in 饲养 (sìyǎng), 'to raise (animals),' and 饲料 (sìliào), 'animal feed.'

components.note: 氵 (water) — thirst is a need for water.
曷 (hé) gives a sound close in rhyme to kě, though the initial consonant has drifted.

example.pinyin: Wǒ hěn kě, xiǎng hē shuǐ.
example.english: I'm very thirsty, I want to drink water.
example.fact: 渴 pairs the water radical with the idea of a need for it — one of the first adjectives beginners learn.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — kissing is done with the mouth.
勿 (wù) gives a sound distantly related to wěn, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 妈妈亲吻了孩子的额头。
example.pinyin: Māma qīnwěn le háizi de étóu.
example.english: Mom kissed the child's forehead.
example.fact: 吻 is most familiar in 亲吻 (qīnwěn), 'to kiss,' and also names 'the lips' in more formal or scientific contexts.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — dressing up and costuming traditionally involve the hands.
分 (fēn) gives a sound distantly related to bàn, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 她在电影里扮演一个医生。
example.pinyin: Tā zài diànyǐng lǐ bànyǎn yí gè yīshēng.
example.english: She plays a doctor in the movie.
example.fact: 扮 is most familiar in 打扮 (dǎban), 'to dress up,' and 扮演 (bànyǎn), 'to play a role.'

etymologyHint: A disobedient 屰 person 辶; 屰 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 辶 (walk, movement) — 逆 describes moving in the wrong or opposite direction.
屰 pictures a person turned upside down, an old image for 'contrary, backwards.'

example.hanzi: 请逆时针转动这个盖子。
example.english: Please turn this lid counterclockwise.
example.fact: 逆 is most familiar in 逆时针 (nìshízhēn), 'counterclockwise,' the opposite of 顺时针 (shùnshízhēn).

etymologyHint: Something dangerous 危 to one's flesh ⺼

components.note: ⺼ (flesh) — 脆 originally described flesh that tears or breaks easily.
危 (dangerous) contributes to the character's form, describing something fragile or easily broken.

example.pinyin: Zhège píngguǒ yòu cuì yòu tián.
example.english: This apple is both crisp and sweet.
example.fact: 脆 describes something crisp or brittle — used for food texture as well as for fragile objects.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — panting and gasping happen through the mouth.
耑 (duān) gives a sound distantly related to chuǎn, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 跑完步后，他喘气很厉害。
example.pinyin: Pǎo wán bù hòu, tā chuǎnqì hěn lìhai.
example.english: After finishing his run, he was panting heavily.
example.fact: 喘 is most familiar in 喘气 (chuǎnqì), 'to pant, to gasp for breath.'

meanings: a cover; a shade; a hood

components.note: 罒 (net) — 罩 originally described a net-like cover or trap.
卓 (zhuó) gives a sound close in initial to zhào, though the rhyme has drifted over time.

example.hanzi: 出门的时候他戴上了口罩。
example.pinyin: Chūmén de shíhou tā dàishàng le kǒuzhào.
example.english: He put on a face mask before going out.
example.fact: 罩 forms the second half of 口罩 (kǒuzhào), 'face mask' — literally a 'cover' for the mouth.

meanings: used in 蘿蔔|萝卜[luo2 bo5]
etymologyHint: A crack on an oracle bone

components.note: 卜 pictures a crack forming on a heated oracle bone — ancient diviners read these cracks to foretell the future, giving 卜 its meaning 'to divine.'

example.english: I like eating radish.
example.fact: 卜 in the tone-3 reading bǔ means 'to divine'; in the neutral tone used here it's just the second syllable of 萝卜 (luóbo), 'radish' — a case where sound and meaning have nothing to do with each other.

etymologyHint: A fire 火 in one's home 户

components.note: 火 (fire) — a stove or furnace holds a fire.
户 (household, door) contributes to the character's form, placing the fire inside the home.

example.english: Mom heats food using the microwave.
example.fact: 炉 names a stove or furnace, and appears in 微波炉 (wēibōlú), 'microwave oven.'

components.note: 木 (wood, tree) — firewood is wood.
此 (cǐ) gives a sound distantly related to chái, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: In the past, people cooked using firewood.
example.fact: 柴 appears in the idiom 柴米油盐 (chái mǐ yóu yán), literally 'firewood, rice, oil, salt' — shorthand for life's basic daily necessities.

components.note: 忄 (heart) — pleasure and delight are feelings of the heart.
俞 (yú) gives the sound — an exact match for 愉.

example.english: Wishing you a pleasant weekend!
example.fact: 愉 is almost always seen in 愉快 (yúkuài), 'happy, pleasant' — a common closing in greetings and wishes.

components.note: 纟 (thread) — rope is made by twisting thread or fiber together.
黾 (mǐn) gives a sound distantly related to shéng, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: He tied up the box with a rope.
example.fact: 绳 is the standard word for 'rope, string,' as in 绳子 (shéngzi).

components.note: ⺼ (flesh) — 胎 originally named an unborn child inside the body.
台 (tái) gives the sound — a close match for tāi, differing only in tone.

example.english: The bicycle's tire is broken.
example.fact: 胎 originally referred to an unborn fetus, but its most common modern use is inside 轮胎 (lúntāi), 'tire.'

components.note: 艹 (grass, plant) — 蓄 originally described storing up plants or grain.
畜 (xù, in this reading) gives the sound — an exact match for 蓄.

example.hanzi: 他每个月都储蓄一些钱。
example.pinyin: Tā měi gè yuè dōu chǔxù yìxiē qián.
example.english: He saves some money every month.
example.fact: 蓄 is most familiar in 储蓄 (chǔxù), 'savings,' extending the plant-radical idea of storing something up over time.

components.note: 目 (eye) — sleep involves closing one's eyes.
民 (mín) gives a sound close to mián, sharing the initial and a similar rhyme.

example.english: Adequate sleep is very important.
example.fact: 眠 is the formal word for 'sleep,' almost always seen in 睡眠 (shuìmián), the noun form of sleeping.

components.note: 立 (to stand) — 竭 describes pushing oneself to the limit while standing firm.
曷 (hé) gives a sound distantly related to jié, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: He did his utmost to help his friend.
example.fact: 竭 is most familiar in 竭尽全力 (jiéjìn quánlì), a set phrase meaning 'to do one's utmost.'

meanings: to feed (an animal, baby, invalid etc)

components.note: 口 (mouth) — both greeting someone and feeding a baby involve the mouth.
畏 (wèi) gives the sound — an exact match for 喂.

example.pinyin: Wèi, qǐngwèn shì Wáng lǎoshī ma?
example.english: Hello, is this Teacher Wang?
example.fact: 喂 is the standard word for answering the phone in Mandarin — the same character also means 'to feed' an animal or baby.

etymologyHint: A man 亻 being hit 夂 on the head 囟

components.note: 亻 (person) — 傻 describes a state of mind a person is in.
囟 (the top of the head), together with a striking motion below, pictures someone being hit on the head — the odd image behind 傻's meaning 'foolish.'

example.english: Don't do silly things.
example.fact: 傻 describes being foolish or silly, milder in tone than calling someone truly stupid.

components.note: ⺗ (heart) — admiration and longing are feelings of the heart.
莫 (mò) gives a sound close to mù, sharing the initial consonant.

example.hanzi: 我很羡慕他的中文水平。
example.pinyin: Wǒ hěn xiànmù tā de Zhōngwén shuǐpíng.
example.english: I really admire his Chinese level.
example.fact: 慕 is most familiar in 羡慕 (xiànmù), 'to envy, admire,' and 仰慕 (yǎngmù), 'to admire greatly.'

components.note: 氵 (water) — muddiness and turbidity describe a state of water.
军 (jūn) gives a sound distantly related to hún, having drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Tā húnshēn dōu shī tòu le.
example.english: He was soaked all over.
example.fact: 浑 is most familiar in 浑身 (húnshēn), 'all over the body' — from an original meaning of 'muddy, mixed together.'

components.note: 女 (woman) — a component whose original link to the meaning has faded, an example of how radicals don't always map cleanly onto meaning.
干 (gān) gives a sound moderately close to jiān, sharing the final but not the initial.

example.hanzi: 这个故事里的坏人很奸诈。
example.pinyin: Zhège gùshi lǐ de huàirén hěn jiānzhà.
example.english: The villain in this story is very crafty and treacherous.
example.fact: 奸 is most familiar in 奸诈 (jiānzhà), 'crafty, treacherous' — a word often used for villains in stories.

meanings: to slap sb on the face
sliding, hinged or detachable flat part of sth
etymologyHint: A feathered 羽 fan in the shape of a folding door 户

components.note: 户 (door) pictures the folding shape a hand-fan shares with a door panel.
羽 (feather) contributes to the character's form, since early fans were made of feathers.

example.hanzi: 夏天很热，她用扇子扇风。
example.pinyin: Xiàtiān hěn rè, tā yòng shànzi shàn fēng.
example.english: Summer is hot, so she fans herself with a fan.
example.fact: 扇 is also the measure word for doors and windows, as in 一扇门 (yí shàn mén), 'a door.'

components.note: 木 (wood) — cabinets are traditionally made of wood.
巨 (jù) gives a sound distantly related to guì, having drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Yīfu dōu fàng zài yīguì lǐ.
example.english: The clothes are all kept in the wardrobe.
example.fact: 柜 is most familiar in 柜子 (guìzi), 'cabinet,' and 衣柜 (yīguì), 'wardrobe.'

components.note: 忄 (heart) — being pleased is a feeling of the heart.
兑 (duì) gives a sound distantly related to yuè, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 她脸上露出喜悦的笑容。
example.pinyin: Tā liǎn shàng lùchū xǐyuè de xiàoróng.
example.english: A joyful smile appeared on her face.
example.fact: 悦 is a literary word for 'pleased,' most often seen today in 喜悦 (xǐyuè, 'joy') and 愉悦 (yúyuè, 'delight').

components.note: 扌 (hand) — blocking someone's path is often done by hand.
兰 (lán) gives the sound — an exact match for 拦.

example.pinyin: Jǐngchá lánzhù le nà liàng chē.
example.english: The police stopped that car.
example.fact: 拦 is most familiar in 拦住 (lánzhù), 'to block, to stop,' and 阻拦 (zǔlán), 'to obstruct.'

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 诞 originally described boastful, exaggerated speech.
延 (yán) gives a sound distantly related to dàn, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: Christmas is coming soon.
example.fact: 诞 appears in 诞生 (dànshēng), 'to be born,' and in 圣诞节 (Shèngdàn Jié), 'Christmas' — literally the 'holy birth festival.'

components.note: 饣 (food) — feeling full is a state tied to having eaten enough food.
包 (bāo) gives the sound — a close match for bǎo, differing only in tone.

example.english: I'm full, thank you.
example.fact: 饱 is the standard word for feeling full after eating.

etymologyHint: Rays 十 emanating from the 日; 乞 provides the pronunciation

components.note: 龺 (a variant image of 日, the sun) shows rays radiating outward, an image tied to warmth and dryness.
乞 rounds out the character's shape; its own meaning 'to beg' plays no part in 乾's sense of 'dry.'

example.english: Everyone, cheers together!
example.fact: 乾 is the traditional-character form used for 'dry' in words like 乾杯 (gānbēi), 'cheers!'; mainland Chinese simplifies this to 干.

components.note: 氵 (water) — steeping, soaking, and bubbles all involve water.
包 (bāo) gives a sound fairly close to pào, sharing the rhyme and differing mainly in aspiration.

example.english: Mom is brewing tea.
example.fact: 泡 is most familiar in 泡茶 (pào chá), 'to brew tea,' and 泡面 (pàomiàn), 'instant noodles.'

components.note: 戎 (weapons) — 贼 originally linked robbery and violence to arms.
贝 (money, from ancient shell currency) gives a sound distantly related to zéi, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: The police caught that thief.
example.fact: 贼 is the standard word for 'thief,' and by extension can describe someone sly or treacherous.

etymologyHint: 亠, 口, and 冖 form a picture of a pavilion; 丁 provides the pronunciation

components.note: 亭 pictures a pavilion — 亠, 口, and 冖 sketch its peaked roof, supports, and platform.
丁 forms the pavilion's post at the base, completing the picture.

example.hanzi: 公园里有一个漂亮的亭子。
example.pinyin: Gōngyuán lǐ yǒu yí gè piàoliang de tíngzi.
example.english: There's a beautiful pavilion in the park.
example.fact: 亭 is most familiar in 亭子 (tíngzi), a small open pavilion often found in Chinese gardens and parks.

components.note: 夕 pictures a crescent moon, an old image for the coming of evening and dusk.

example.hanzi: 除夕那天，全家人一起吃饭。
example.pinyin: Chúxī nà tiān, quánjiā rén yìqǐ chīfàn.
example.english: On New Year's Eve, the whole family eats together.
example.fact: 夕 alone means 'evening, dusk,' and is most familiar today in 除夕 (chúxī), Chinese New Year's Eve.

components.note: 父 (father) — 爹 names a family relation, one's father.
多 (duō) gives a sound moderately close to diē, sharing the initial consonant.

example.english: He calls his father 'Die' (Dad).
example.fact: 爹 is an older or regional word for 'father,' now mostly heard in rural dialects, historical dramas, or replaced elsewhere by the more common 爸爸 (bàba).

components.note: 酉 (wine) — 酬 originally described toasting someone with wine.
州 (zhōu) gives a sound fairly close to chóu, sharing the rhyme.

example.hanzi: 他做这份工作的报酬很高。
example.pinyin: Tā zuò zhè fèn gōngzuò de bàochou hěn gāo.
example.english: The pay for this job is very high.
example.fact: 酬 is most familiar in 报酬 (bàochou), 'payment, reward' for work done.

components.note: 亻 (person) — a Confucian scholar is a person of learning.
需 (xū) gives a sound distantly related to rú, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 儒家思想影响了中国几千年。
example.pinyin: Rújiā sīxiǎng yǐngxiǎng le Zhōngguó jǐ qiān nián.
example.english: Confucian thought has influenced China for thousands of years.
example.fact: 儒 names a Confucian scholar, and appears in 儒家 (Rújiā), 'Confucianism.'

etymologyHint: A woman 女 related by 因 marriage

components.note: 女 (woman) — 姻 describes a relationship formed through marriage.
因 (cause, reason — here 'by virtue of') contributes to the character's form, describing a bond created by marriage.

example.english: Marriage needs effort from both sides.
example.fact: 姻 is almost always seen paired with 婚 in 婚姻 (hūnyīn), 'marriage.'

components.note: 卵 pictures a pair of small round eggs — the image behind its meaning 'egg, ovum.'

example.english: Fish eggs can hatch into little fish.
example.fact: 卵 is the more scientific or literary word for 'egg, ovum'; the everyday word for a chicken egg is 蛋 (dàn), not 卵.

components.note: 气 (air, gas) — atmosphere and mood are described using the word for air.
分 (fēn) gives the sound — an exact match for 氛.

example.pinyin: Shēngrì pàiduì de qìfēn hěn hǎo.
example.english: The atmosphere of the birthday party is great.
example.fact: 氛 is almost always seen in 气氛 (qìfēn), 'atmosphere, mood.'

components.note: 氵 (water) — leaking is described using the water radical, whether literal or figurative.
世 (shì) gives a sound distantly related to xiè, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 别把这个秘密泄露出去。
example.pinyin: Bié bǎ zhège mìmì xièlù chūqù.
example.english: Don't leak this secret.
example.fact: 泄 is most familiar in 泄露 (xièlù), 'to leak, to divulge (information).'

meanings: classifier for long objects such as guns

components.note: 木 (wood) — a pole or shaft was traditionally made of wood.
干 (gān) gives the sound — an exact match for 杆.

example.pinyin: Xuéxiào ménkǒu yǒu yì gēn qígān.
example.english: There's a flagpole at the school entrance.
example.fact: 杆 is most familiar in 旗杆 (qígān), 'flagpole,' and 电线杆 (diànxiàn'gān), 'utility pole.'

components.note: 扌 (hand) — being close by is described using a hand-related radical.
矣 (yǐ) gives a sound distantly related to āi, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: He sits next to me.
example.fact: 挨 read āi means 'next to, close by'; the same character read ái means 'to endure, to suffer' — a useful tone to keep straight.

components.note: 亻 (person) — a monk is a person.
曾 (céng) gives a sound fairly close to sēng, sharing the rhyme.

example.pinyin: Sìmiào lǐ zhùzhe jǐ wèi sēngrén.
example.english: A few monks live in the temple.
example.fact: 僧 is the more formal word for a Buddhist monk, often used alongside the more colloquial 和尚 (héshang).

components.note: 虫 (insect) — honey is made by bees, which are insects.
宓 (mì) gives the sound — an exact match for 蜜.

example.hanzi: 我喜欢在牛奶里加蜂蜜。
example.pinyin: Wǒ xǐhuan zài niúnǎi lǐ jiā fēngmì.
example.english: I like adding honey to milk.
example.fact: 蜜 is almost always seen in 蜂蜜 (fēngmì), 'honey,' literally 'bee-sweetness.'

components.note: 口 (mouth) — reciting and chanting are done aloud.
今 (jīn) gives a sound moderately close to yín, sharing a similar rhyme.

example.english: Poets like to recite poetry.
example.fact: 吟 is most familiar in 吟诗 (yínshī), 'to chant or recite poetry.'

components.note: 犭 (animal) — 猩 names a kind of animal.
星 (xīng) gives the sound — an exact match for 猩.

example.pinyin: Dòngwùyuán lǐ yǒu yì zhī xīngxīng.
example.english: There's an orangutan at the zoo.
example.fact: 猩 rarely stands alone; it's almost always doubled into 猩猩 (xīngxīng), 'orangutan, ape.'

meanings: used in 半身不遂[ban4 shen1 bu4 sui2]

components.note: 辶 (walk, movement) — 遂 relates to following a path through to completion.
豕 (shǐ) gives a sound distantly related to suì, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: He finally had his wish fulfilled.
example.fact: 遂 is mostly literary today; in everyday speech, 'to fulfill a wish' is usually expressed with 如愿 (rúyuàn) rather than 遂.

components.note: 犭 (dog, generic animal radical) — an old classification whose link to 'narrow' has faded over time.
夹 (jiā) gives a sound moderately close to xiá, sharing a similar rhyme.

example.english: This road is very narrow.
example.fact: 狭 is almost always seen in 狭窄 (xiázhǎi), 'narrow,' whether describing a road or a narrow-minded view.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh) — resemblance here is tied to physical, bodily likeness.
⺌ (a form related to 小, 'small') gives the sound — a close match for xiào, differing only in tone.

example.english: What's your zodiac animal?
example.fact: 肖 means 'to resemble,' and gives its name to 生肖 (shēngxiào), the twelve zodiac animals.

etymologyHint: Something tasty 甘 to the tongue 舌

components.note: 舌 (tongue) — taste is sensed on the tongue.
甘 (sweet, tasty) contributes to the character's form, naming the flavor itself.

example.english: This fruit is very sweet.
example.fact: 甜 is the standard word for 'sweet,' one of the first taste adjectives beginners learn.

meanings: rose-tinted sky or clouds at sunrise or sunset

components.note: 雨 (rain) — 霞 names a sky phenomenon related to clouds and weather.
叚 (jiǎ) gives a sound moderately close to xiá, sharing a similar rhyme.

example.english: The sunset glow in the evening is beautiful.
example.fact: 霞 is most familiar in 晚霞 (wǎnxiá), 'sunset glow,' and 朝霞 (zhāoxiá), 'dawn glow.'

components.note: 马 (horse) — 驳 originally described a horse with a mottled, mixed coat color.
爻 (yáo) gives a sound distantly related to bó, having drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Tā fǎnbó le lǎoshī de guāndiǎn.
example.english: He refuted the teacher's viewpoint.
example.fact: 驳 is most familiar in 反驳 (fǎnbó), 'to refute, to argue back.'

components.note: 衤 (clothes) — abundance was traditionally shown through ample clothing.
谷 (gǔ) gives a sound distantly related to yù, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 现在很多家庭都比较富裕。
example.pinyin: Xiànzài hěn duō jiātíng dōu bǐjiào fùyù.
example.english: Nowadays many families are relatively affluent.
example.fact: 裕 is almost always seen in 富裕 (fùyù), 'wealthy, affluent.'

components.note: 页 (head) — 顽 originally described a quality of the head, i.e. stubbornness of mind.
元 (yuán) gives a sound fairly close to wán, sharing the rhyme.

example.english: This child is very naughty.
example.fact: 顽 is most familiar in 顽皮 (wánpí), 'naughty, mischievous,' and 顽固 (wángù), 'stubborn.'

example.english: His surname is Yu.
example.fact: 於 is an old, traditional variant of the preposition 于 ('at, in'); today it's mostly seen as a surname or in formal, literary phrasing.

meanings: to borrow money at a time of urgent need
etymologyHint: To pick 扌 a fruit off a branch 啇

components.note: 扌 (hand) — picking fruit is done by hand.
啇 (root of 蒂, a fruit's stem) contributes to the character's form, naming what the fruit is picked from.

example.pinyin: Tā zài guǒyuán lǐ zhāi píngguǒ.
example.english: He is picking apples in the orchard.
example.fact: 摘 is the standard verb for picking fruit or flowers, and by extension, for selecting or picking out an item (as in 摘要, 'summary').

components.note: 矢 (arrow, dart) — an old link between measuring length and the character's meaning.
委 (wěi) gives a sound distantly related to ǎi, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: This person is short.
example.fact: 矮 is the standard word for describing a person's short height.

components.note: 禾 (grain) — 秒 originally named the delicate beard of a grain stalk.
少 (shǎo) gives a sound moderately close to miǎo, sharing the rhyme.

example.english: There are sixty seconds in a minute.
example.fact: 秒 originally meant the fine beard on a stalk of grain, later extended to the smallest common unit of time, the 'second.'

example.pinyin: 'Qīng' shì gǔdài duì guānyuán de chēnghu.
example.english: 'Qing' was an ancient term used to address officials.
example.fact: 卿 was historically a title for a high-ranking official, and also an old term of endearment between spouses — today it survives mainly in period dramas and classical texts.

components.note: 田 (field, farm) — livestock are raised on a farm.
玄 (xuán) gives a sound distantly related to chù, having drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Niú hé yáng dōu shì jiāchù.
example.english: Cows and sheep are both livestock.
example.fact: 畜 read chù means 'livestock' (as in 家畜); the same character read xù means 'to raise animals,' as in 畜牧 (xùmù).

components.note: 口 (mouth) — swallowing and the throat both involve the mouth.
因 (yīn) gives a sound moderately close to yàn, sharing the initial consonant.

example.english: He slowly swallowed the medicine.
example.fact: 咽 has three readings — yān ('throat,' a noun), yàn ('to swallow'), and yè ('to choke up') — this entry uses the yàn 'to swallow' reading.

etymologyHint: To put on 扌 fur 皮; 皮 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 扌 (hand) — draping a garment over the shoulders is done with the hands.
皮 (fur, skin) contributes to the character's form, naming what early garments were made of.

example.pinyin: Tiān lěng le, tā pī shàng le wàitào.
example.english: It got cold, so she draped a coat over her shoulders.
example.fact: 披 is most familiar in 披上 (pī shàng), 'to drape (a garment) over oneself.'

components.note: 车 (cart) — 辅 originally named a wooden support fitted to a cart wheel.
甫 (fǔ) gives the sound — an exact match for 辅.

example.english: The teacher tutors us after class.
example.fact: 辅 is most familiar in 辅导 (fǔdǎo), 'to tutor, to coach,' and 辅助 (fǔzhù), 'to assist.'

example.pinyin: Qǐng zài zhèngquè dá'àn shàng dǎ gōu.
example.english: Please put a checkmark on the correct answer.
example.fact: 勾 is most familiar today in 打勾 (dǎ gōu), 'to put a checkmark,' a common instruction on tests and forms.

components.note: 皿 (dish, container) — a basin or pot is a kind of container.
分 (fēn) gives a sound moderately close to pén, sharing the rhyme.

example.pinyin: Yángtái shàng yǒu hěn duō huāpén.
example.english: There are many flowerpots on the balcony.
example.fact: 盆 is most familiar in 花盆 (huāpén), 'flowerpot,' and 脸盆 (liǎnpén), 'washbasin.'

etymologyHint: A bow 弓 and arrow 土 used to defend a border 畺; 畺 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 弓 (bow) — a border was historically defended with bows.
畺 pictures fields laid out in rows, marking off a boundary — the image behind 疆's meaning 'border.'

example.english: Xinjiang is in the northwest of China.
example.fact: 疆 means 'border, frontier,' and gives its name to 新疆 (Xīnjiāng), literally 'new frontier.'

components.note: 贝 (money) — gambling involves staking money.
者 (zhě) gives a sound distantly related to dǔ, having drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Dǔbó shì bù hǎo de xíguàn.
example.english: Gambling is a bad habit.
example.fact: 赌 is almost always seen in 赌博 (dǔbó), 'to gamble.'

components.note: 土 (earth) — sculpting was traditionally done with clay, a form of earth.
朔 (shuò) gives a sound moderately close to sù, sharing the initial consonant family.

example.pinyin: Zhège bēizi shì sùliào zuò de.
example.english: This cup is made of plastic.
example.fact: 塑 originally meant to model something in clay; today it's most common in 塑料 (sùliào), 'plastic.'

etymologyHint: A monster with a scary head 田

components.note: 田 here pictures a large, frightening head — part of an old image of a masked, monstrous figure that gave 畏 its meaning 'to fear, dread.'

example.pinyin: Tā yìdiǎn yě bù wèijù kùnnan.
example.english: He isn't afraid of difficulties at all.
example.fact: 畏 is most familiar in 畏惧 (wèijù), 'to fear,' and 无所畏惧 (wúsuǒ wèijù), 'utterly fearless.'

components.note: 口 (mouth) — arguing is done vocally.
少 (shǎo) gives a sound fairly close to chǎo, sharing the rhyme.

example.english: The two of them argued again.
example.fact: 吵 is most familiar in 吵架 (chǎojià), 'to quarrel,' and 吵闹 (chǎonào), 'noisy.'

meanings: used in 囊膪[nang1 chuai4] and 囊揣[nang1 chuai4]
used in 鼓鼓囊囊[gu3 gu5 nang1 nang1]

components.note: 口 here represents the opening of a sack or pouch.
襄 (xiāng) gives a sound distantly related to náng, having drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Yīshēng gěi le wǒ yí hé jiāonáng.
example.english: The doctor gave me a box of capsules.
example.fact: 囊 means 'sack, pouch,' and today is most familiar in 胶囊 (jiāonáng), 'capsule' (as in medicine).

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 嗯 is a vocalized grunt or interjection.
恩 (ēn) gives a loosely related sound; as an onomatopoeic grunt, 嗯's pronunciation doesn't follow the usual sound-change patterns.

example.english: Huh? What did you say?
example.fact: 嗯 changes meaning with its tone: ń (rising) shows surprise or asks 'huh?', while ǹ (falling) simply means 'yeah, okay.'

components.note: 氵 (water) — a lake, and mooring a boat, both involve water.
白 (bái) gives a sound moderately close to pō, sharing the initial consonant family.

example.hanzi: 中国有很多美丽的湖泊。
example.pinyin: Zhōngguó yǒu hěn duō měilì de húpō.
example.english: China has many beautiful lakes.
example.fact: 泊 read pō appears in 湖泊 (húpō), 'lakes'; the same character read bó means 'to moor a boat' or 'to park,' as in 停泊 (tíngbó).

components.note: ⺼ (flesh) — lungs are a body organ.
巿 (a rare character) gives a sound distantly related to fèi, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: Smoking is bad for the lungs.
example.fact: 肺 is the standard word for 'lungs,' a body organ.

components.note: 马 (horse) — 骤 originally described a horse galloping.
聚 (jù) gives a sound distantly related to zhòu, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: The weather suddenly turned cold.
example.fact: 骤 is most familiar in 骤然 (zhòurán), 'suddenly,' from an original meaning tied to a horse's fast gallop.

components.note: 纟 (thread) — winding and wrapping are described using the thread radical.
㢆 (a rare character) gives the sound — an exact match for 缠.

example.english: The vine winds around the big tree.
example.fact: 缠 is most familiar in 缠绕 (chánrào), 'to wind around,' and 纠缠 (jiūchán), 'to pester, get entangled with.'

etymologyHint: Simplified form of 岡, clouds 网 forming over a mountain 山

components.note: 冈 is the simplified form of 岡, which pictured a mountain ridge under a cap of cloud — the image behind its meaning 'ridge, mound.'

example.hanzi: 井冈山是一个有名的地方。
example.pinyin: Jǐnggāngshān shì yí gè yǒumíng de dìfang.
example.english: Jinggangshan is a famous place.
example.fact: 冈 means a hill ridge, and is part of the place name 井冈山 (Jǐnggāngshān), a mountain range in Jiangxi province.

etymologyHint: An ugly 丑 sheep 羊

components.note: 羊 (sheep) — 羞 pairs a sheep with the idea of something unsightly.
丑 (ugly, shameful) contributes to the character's form, giving 羞 its meaning 'ashamed, shy.'

example.hanzi: 小女孩看到生人有点害羞。
example.pinyin: Xiǎo nǚhái kàndào shēngrén yǒudiǎn hàixiū.
example.english: The little girl feels a bit shy seeing strangers.
example.fact: 羞 is almost always seen in 害羞 (hàixiū), 'shy, bashful.'

components.note: 目 (eye) — glaring and staring are actions of the eyes.
登 (dēng) gives the sound — a close match for dèng, differing only in tone.

example.pinyin: Tā shēngqì de dèng le wǒ yì yǎn.
example.english: He glared at me angrily.
example.fact: 瞪 is most familiar in 瞪眼 (dèng yǎn), 'to glare, to open one's eyes wide.'

example.hanzi: 客厅里挂着一个漂亮的吊灯。
example.pinyin: Kètīng lǐ guàzhe yí gè piàoliang de diàodēng.
example.english: A beautiful hanging lamp hangs in the living room.
example.fact: 吊 is most familiar in 吊灯 (diàodēng), 'hanging lamp, chandelier,' and generally means 'to hang, to suspend.'

components.note: 贝 (money) — trade and merchants are tied to money.
覀 (a variant form of 西) gives a sound distantly related to jiǎ, having drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Jiǎ shì yí gè chángjiàn de xìng.
example.english: Jia is a common surname.
example.fact: 贾 read jiǎ is a surname; the same character read gǔ means 'merchant, to trade' — as in the classical word 商贾 (shānggǔ), 'merchants.'

etymologyHint: Water 氵 falling like raindrops 雨; 屚 provides the pronunciation

components.note: 氵 (water) — 漏 describes water escaping through a gap.
屚 pictures rain seeping in through a roof, the image behind 漏's meaning 'to leak.'

example.english: The roof is leaking water.
example.fact: 漏 is most familiar in 漏水 (lòu shuǐ), 'to leak water.'

etymologyHint: Markings 文 in jade 王

components.note: 王 (jade), appearing twice, pictures two pieces of jade.
文 (markings, pattern) sits between them, showing decorative markings running through the jade — the image behind 斑's meaning 'mottled, spotted.'

example.pinyin: Tā liǎn shàng yǒu yìxiē quèbān.
example.english: He has some freckles on his face.
example.fact: 斑 is most familiar in 斑点 (bāndiǎn), 'spot, speck,' and 雀斑 (quèbān), 'freckle.'

components.note: 氵 (water) — big waves are a feature of water.
寿 (shòu) gives a sound distantly related to tāo, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: The waves by the sea are very big.
example.fact: 涛 is most familiar in 波涛 (bōtāo), 'billows, big waves,' and is a common character in given names.

components.note: 心 (heart) — a leisurely state of mind is a feeling of the heart.
攸 (yōu) gives the sound — an exact match for 悠.

example.english: China has a long history.
example.fact: 悠 is most familiar in 悠久 (yōujiǔ), 'long-standing' (for history or tradition), and 悠闲 (yōuxián), 'leisurely.'

etymologyHint: A deer with an antlered head, two legs, and a tail

components.note: 鹿 is a simplified picture of a deer, with its antlered head, long legs, and tail all visible in the strokes.

example.pinyin: Sēnlín lǐ yǒu yì zhī lù.
example.english: There's a deer in the forest.
example.fact: 鹿 appears in the idiom 指鹿为马 (zhǐ lù wéi mǎ), 'calling a deer a horse' — describing a deliberate lie that everyone is forced to go along with.

components.note: 亻 (person) — a prisoner of war is a person.
孚 (fú) gives the sound — an exact match for 俘.

example.pinyin: Shìbīng zhuādào le jǐ míng fúlǔ.
example.english: The soldiers captured several prisoners.
example.fact: 俘 is almost always seen in 俘虏 (fúlǔ), 'captive, prisoner of war' (as a noun), or 'to capture' (as a verb).

components.note: 钅 (metal) — tin is a metal.
易 (yì) gives a sound distantly related to xī, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 无锡是江苏的一个城市。
example.pinyin: Wúxī shì Jiāngsū de yí gè chéngshì.
example.english: Wuxi is a city in Jiangsu.
example.fact: 锡 names the metal tin, and gives its name to the city 无锡 (Wúxī) in Jiangsu province — literally 'without tin.'

etymologyHint: A hand 又(altered) holding an empty shell 甲 (altered)

components.note: 卑 traditionally pictures a hand holding an empty, lowly object — an old image behind its meaning 'low, humble.'

example.hanzi: 他因为成绩不好感到自卑。
example.pinyin: Tā yīnwèi chéngjì bù hǎo gǎndào zìbēi.
example.english: He feels inferior because of his bad grades.
example.fact: 卑 is most familiar in 自卑 (zìbēi), 'feeling inferior,' and 卑鄙 (bēibǐ), 'despicable.'

etymologyHint: A corpse 死 laid 廾 to rest under the grass 艹

components.note: 艹 (grass) — 葬 pictures a burial taking place under the grass.
死 (death, corpse) contributes to the character's form, naming who is being laid to rest.
廾 (two hands) shows the corpse being carefully laid down, completing the picture behind 葬's meaning 'to bury.'

example.english: The funeral was held at the church.
example.fact: 葬 is most familiar in 葬礼 (zànglǐ), 'funeral,' and 埋葬 (máizàng), 'to bury.'

etymologyHint: To carve 钅 one's name 名; 名 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 钅 (metal) — inscriptions were traditionally carved into metal or stone.
名 (name) contributes to the character's form, describing what gets carved or engraved.

example.pinyin: Zhè jù huà shì wǒ de zuòyòumíng.
example.english: This sentence is my motto.
example.fact: 铭 is most familiar in 座右铭 (zuòyòumíng), 'motto,' literally 'inscription at the right of one's seat.'

etymologyHint: Difficult 难 waters 氵 to navigate; 难 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 氵 (water) — a beach or sandbar is found at the water's edge.
难 (difficult) contributes to the character's form, describing waters that are tricky to navigate near a shoal.

example.hanzi: 夏天我们喜欢去沙滩玩。
example.pinyin: Xiàtiān wǒmen xǐhuan qù shātān wán.
example.english: In summer we like to go play at the beach.
example.fact: 滩 is almost always seen in 沙滩 (shātān), 'beach, sandy shore.'

components.note: 女 (woman) — 嫁 specifically describes a woman marrying.
家 (jiā) gives the sound — a close match for jià, differing only in tone.

example.pinyin: Tā míngnián yào jià gěi tā le.
example.english: She's going to marry him next year.
example.fact: 嫁 specifically describes a woman marrying into her husband's family, while 娶 (qǔ) describes a man taking a wife — two different verbs where English just uses 'marry.'

components.note: 亻 (person) — urging is something one person does to another.
崔 (cuī) gives the sound — an exact match for 催.

example.pinyin: Māma cuī wǒ kuài diǎn qǐchuáng.
example.english: Mom is urging me to get up quickly.
example.fact: 催 is almost always seen in 催促 (cuīcù), 'to urge, to press (someone to hurry).'

etymologyHint: An orbiting 旋 gem 王; 旋 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 王 (jade) — 璇 names a kind of fine jade.
旋 (to spin, orbit) contributes to the character's form, linking the gem to the idea of a star's orbit.

example.hanzi: 璇是一个常见的女孩名字。
example.pinyin: Xuán shì yí gè chángjiàn de nǚhái míngzi.
example.english: Xuan is a common girl's name.
example.fact: 璇 names a type of beautiful jade and today is used almost exclusively in given names, especially for girls.

meanings: (bound form) wing (of a bird or insect)

components.note: 羽 (feather) — a wing is covered in feathers.
支 (zhī) gives a sound fairly close to chì, sharing a similar rhyme.

example.english: Birds fly using their wings.
example.fact: 翅 is almost always seen in 翅膀 (chìbǎng), 'wing.'

components.note: 皿 (dish, container) — a box is a kind of container.
合 (hé) gives the sound — an exact match for 盒.

example.english: There's chocolate in this box.
example.fact: 盒 is the standard word for a small box or case, as in 盒子 (hézi).

components.note: 亦 (also, similarly) contributes to the character's form.
虫 (insect) sits below it — an old, dismissive way of grouping outsiders with lowly creatures, behind 蛮's meaning 'barbarian.'

example.english: This place is quite pretty.
example.fact: 蛮 historically meant 'barbarian, uncivilized' (as in 野蛮, yěmán); in colloquial speech today it's also used as a casual intensifier meaning 'quite, rather,' as in 蛮好 (mán hǎo).

meanings: classical final particle, similar to modern 了[le5]

example.english: It is already too late.
example.fact: 矣 is a classical Chinese sentence-final particle, similar to modern 了 — it doesn't appear in everyday speech, but survives in set phrases like 为时已晚矣, 'it's already too late.'

meanings: water in which rice has been rinsed
a river that flows into the Han
(archaic) water in which rice has been washed

components.note: 氵 (water) — 潘 originally named the water used to rinse rice.
番 (fān) gives a sound fairly close to pān, sharing the rhyme.

example.english: Pan is his surname.
example.fact: 潘 today is used almost exclusively as a surname; its old meaning refers to the water left over from rinsing rice.

components.note: 止 (stop, foot) — a fork in the road is about a path one walks.
支 (zhī) gives a sound distantly related to qí, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 他们在这个问题上有分歧。
example.pinyin: Tāmen zài zhège wèntí shàng yǒu fēnqí.
example.english: They have a disagreement on this issue.
example.fact: 歧 is almost always seen in 分歧 (fēnqí), 'disagreement, divergence (of views).'

meanings: (bound form) to confer; to bestow; to grant

components.note: 贝 (money) — bestowing a gift is tied to giving something of value.
易 (yì) gives a sound distantly related to cì, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 古代皇帝常常赐给大臣礼物。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài huángdì chángcháng cì gěi dàchén lǐwù.
example.english: Ancient emperors often bestowed gifts on their officials.
example.fact: 赐 is a formal, literary word for 'to bestow, to grant' — historically describing a ruler giving gifts to subjects.

components.note: 鱼 (fish) — abalone is a sea creature, grouped with the fish radical.
包 (bāo) gives the sound — a close match for bào, differing only in tone.

example.pinyin: Bào shì yí gè Zhōngguó xìng.
example.english: Bao is a Chinese surname.
example.fact: 鲍 names the sea snail abalone (鲍鱼), a prized delicacy in Chinese cuisine, and is also a common surname.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — pots and pans are made of metal.
呙 (guō) gives the sound — an exact match for 锅.

example.english: Mom stir-fries with a pan.
example.fact: 锅 is the standard word for a cooking pot, pan, or wok.

components.note: 广 (a building, shelter) — a corridor is part of a building.
郎 (láng) gives the sound — an exact match for 廊.

example.pinyin: Jiàoshì wàimiàn yǒu yì tiáo zǒuláng.
example.english: There's a corridor outside the classroom.
example.fact: 廊 is almost always seen in 走廊 (zǒuláng), 'corridor, hallway.'

components.note: 扌 (hand) — tearing something open is done by hand.
斥 (chì) gives a sound moderately close to chāi, sharing the initial consonant.

example.english: He unwrapped his birthday present.
example.fact: 拆 is most familiar in 拆开 (chāikāi), 'to open, unwrap,' and 拆迁 (chāiqiān), 'to demolish and relocate.'

components.note: 氵 (water) — irrigation and pouring both involve water.
雚 (an ancestor of characters like 观 and 权) gives a sound close to guàn.

example.english: Farmers use water to irrigate the fields.
example.fact: 灌 is almost always seen in 灌溉 (guàngài), 'to irrigate.'

components.note: 力 (strength) — making an effort is tied to exerting strength.
免 (miǎn) gives the sound — an exact match for 勉.

example.english: He barely passed the exam.
example.fact: 勉 is most familiar in 勉强 (miǎnqiǎng), 'reluctantly, barely,' and 勤勉 (qínmiǎn), 'diligent.'

etymologyHint: Losing 亡 one's sight 目; 亡 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 亡 (loss, death — here 'losing') contributes to the character's form, describing losing one's sight.
目 (eye) sits below it, naming the sense that is lost — giving 盲 its meaning 'blind.'

example.english: Blind people read Braille with their hands.
example.fact: 盲 also names 盲文 (Mángwén), the Chinese term for Braille.

meanings: to slaughter; to butcher; to kill (animals etc)
(coll.) to fleece; to rip off; to overcharge
etymologyHint: A barracks 宀 where slaves 辛 live

components.note: 宀 (roof, house) — 宰 originally pictured an official's residence.
辛 (bitter, hard labor) contributes to the character's form, referring to the servants who worked there — giving 宰 its meanings 'to govern' and 'to slaughter.'

example.pinyin: Gǔdài de zǎixiàng quánlì hěn dà.
example.english: Ancient prime ministers had great power.
example.fact: 宰 is most familiar in 宰相 (zǎixiàng), the historical title for a prime minister, and 屠宰 (túzǎi), 'to slaughter.'
